description: Potato is a cool-season tuber crop grown mainly in the rabi season on the Indo-Gangetic plains and in summer in the hills. It grows best at 15-25 °C, and tubers form best when nights are below 20 °C.
npk_split: Basal at planting: 1/2 N + full P2O5 + full K2O placed in furrows; remaining 1/2 N at earthing-up, 25-30 days after planting (range 150-180 : 80-100 : 100-120 kg/ha depending on soil and variety).

Bacterial wilt.name: Bacterial Wilt
Bacterial wilt.description: Bacterial wilt (brown rot) is a soil- and tuber-borne disease that wilts potato plants and rots tubers in warm, moist soils. Infected seed tubers carry it to new fields, and no spray can cure an infected plant.
symptoms: Sudden wilting of leaves, first on one stem or at the top, while they are still green
Plants wilt in the day and partly recover at night before collapsing
Brown ring inside the cut stem base and in cut tubers
Milky white ooze from the cut stem, the tuber ring or the tuber eyes, with soil sticking to the eyes
Bacterial wilt.spread: Carried in infected seed tubers and surviving in soil, crop residue and weed hosts; spreads through irrigation water, cut-seed knives and root wounds, and is favoured by warm (25-35 °C), wet soil.
Bacterial wilt.action: Uproot wilted plants with their tubers and surrounding soil and destroy them, and do not keep any tubers from this field as seed; no spray cures bacterial wilt.

treatment.name: Healthy whole seed tubers
treatment.notes: Plant certified, uncut seed tubers; cutting tubers spreads the bacteria on the knife.

treatment.name: Stable bleaching powder
treatment.notes: Mix with fertilizer and apply in the furrows at planting in fields with a wilt history (ICAR-CPRI practice).

treatment.name: Rotation with cereals
treatment.notes: Grow maize, wheat or other cereals; keep tomato, brinjal and chilli off the same land.

Early blight.name: Early Blight
Early blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease of potato that starts on older, lower leaves, especially on stressed or under-fed plants. Severe defoliation reduces tuber size, and tubers can develop dark, sunken lesions.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves
Spots are often angular, limited by veins, with a yellow halo
Leaves yellow, dry and drop from the bottom of the plant upward
Dark, dry, sunken lesions on tubers
Early blight.spread: Survives in infected crop debris, soil and solanaceous weeds; spores spread by wind, rain splash and workers; favoured by warm weather (24-29 °C), alternating wet and dry spells and stressed, under-fed plants.
Early blight.action: Spray Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 g/L) now, repeat every 7-10 days, and remove infected lower leaves.

treatment.name: Rotate away from solanaceous crops
treatment.notes: Potato, tomato, brinjal and chilli share this fungus; remove solanaceous weeds as well.

Insect damage.name: Insect Damage
Insect damage.cause: Unspecified chewing or sucking insects, such as hadda beetle (Henosepilachna vigintioctopunctata), cutworm (Agrotis ipsilon), leaf-eating caterpillar (Spodoptera litura), aphids (Myzus persicae) and leafhoppers
Insect damage.description: This class covers feeding injury by chewing or sucking insects on potato leaves; the photo cannot tell which species is responsible. Light leaf feeding rarely cuts tuber yield, so identify the insect before spraying.
symptoms: Irregular holes or ragged, eaten leaf edges
Leaf surface scraped into a net-like pattern (hadda beetle)
Young plants cut at ground level (cutworm)
Curled or puckered leaves with small insects on the underside (aphids, leafhoppers)
Insects, eggs or droppings on the leaf underside
Insect damage.spread: Adults fly or crawl in from weeds, neighbouring crops and crop residue, and numbers build up in warm weather on lush, heavily fertilised crops.
Insect damage.action: Check both leaf surfaces in the early morning or evening to find the insect, hand-pick beetles and caterpillars, and spray neem oil 1500 ppm 3-5 ml/L if fresh damage keeps appearing.

treatment.name: Identify the insect first
treatment.notes: Chewed holes mean beetles or caterpillars; curled leaves with tiny insects underneath mean aphids or leafhoppers.

treatment.name: Neem oil 1500 ppm
treatment.notes: First spray for light damage by any of these insects; cover leaf undersides.

treatment.name: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL
treatment.notes: Only for confirmed aphids or leafhoppers, which also spread potato viruses; max 2 sprays per season, avoid during flowering (bees).

Late blight.name: Late Blight
Late blight.description: Late blight is the most destructive potato disease (cause of the Irish famine) and can destroy a field within 7-10 days in cool, wet weather. It attacks leaves, stems and tubers, which rot in the field and in storage.
symptoms: Pale green, water-soaked spots, often starting at leaf tips and margins, that quickly turn dark brown to black
White, downy growth on the underside of lesions in humid mornings
Dark lesions on stems and petioles; foliage collapses with a foul smell
Reddish-brown dry rot under the skin of tubers
Late blight.spread: Airborne sporangia travel kilometres on wind and rain from infected potato/tomato fields, cull piles, volunteer plants and infected seed tubers; cool nights (10-20 °C), humidity above 90% and long leaf wetness cause explosive epidemics.
Late blight.action: Act immediately: spray Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (2.5 g/L), remove and destroy infected plants, and warn neighbouring growers.

treatment.name: Certified seed and high earthing-up
treatment.notes: Use certified disease-free seed tubers, earth up well, and cut haulms 10-15 days before harvest so that tubers are not infected.

treatment.name: Blight-resistant varieties
treatment.notes: Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Himalini and Kufri Chipsona-1 carry late blight resistance; ask your KVK which variety suits your area.

Nematode damage.name: Nematode Damage
Nematode damage.cause: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica) and potato cyst nematodes (Globodera rostochiensis, G. pallida)
Nematode damage.description: Nematodes are microscopic soil worms that feed on potato roots and tubers, so the damage seen on leaves is the result of a weak root system. Root-knot nematodes occur widely, while potato cyst nematodes are a quarantine pest of hill areas such as the Nilgiris.
symptoms: Patches of stunted plants with pale yellow leaves
Plants wilt at midday even when the soil is moist
Swellings (galls) on roots, or pinhead-sized white to golden cysts on roots
Pimple-like warts on the tuber skin
Early drying of the crop with few, small tubers
Nematode damage.spread: Carried in soil on tools, footwear and machinery, in irrigation water and on infected seed tubers, and builds up when potato or other host crops are grown year after year.
Nematode damage.action: Uproot a few weak plants and check the roots for galls or cysts, then plan a 3-4 year rotation with non-host crops, because no leaf spray controls nematodes.

treatment.name: Rotation with non-host crops
treatment.notes: Cereals, cabbage, radish and garlic do not host potato cyst nematode; keep tomato and brinjal out of the rotation.

treatment.name: Clean seed tubers
treatment.notes: Do not use seed tubers from infested fields; moving seed potato out of cyst-nematode areas is restricted by quarantine.

treatment.name: Resistant variety
treatment.notes: Kufri Swarna resists potato cyst nematode in the Nilgiris; ask your KVK about varieties for your area.

Viral disease.name: Viral Disease
Viral disease.cause: Virus complex: Potato virus Y, Potato leafroll virus, Potato virus X, S and A, and Tomato leaf curl New Delhi virus (apical leaf curl)
Viral disease.description: Potato is attacked by a complex of viruses that pass from crop to crop in seed tubers, which is why farm-saved seed degenerates and yields fall each year. The photo cannot tell which virus is present, and there is no cure for an infected plant.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottling (mosaic) on leaves
Leaflets rolled upward, stiff and leathery (leafroll)
Crinkled, puckered leaves, sometimes with dark dead streaks on the veins
Top leaves curled and yellow-mottled (apical leaf curl)
Stunted plants with few, small tubers
Viral disease.spread: Carried mainly in infected seed tubers and spread in the field by aphids (virus Y, leafroll), whiteflies (apical leaf curl) and, for viruses X and S, by contact with plants, tools and cut-seed knives.
Viral disease.action: No cure: uproot and remove infected plants together with their tubers, and do not save seed from this crop.
Viral disease.vector: Aphids (Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii); whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) for apical leaf curl

treatment.name: Certified seed tubers
treatment.notes: Replace farm-saved seed with certified seed; most potato virus comes in with the seed tubers.

treatment.name: Early haulm cutting in seed crops
treatment.dose: When aphids reach 20 per 100 compound leaves
treatment.notes: Cut the haulms of a seed crop at this aphid count so that late virus infection does not reach the tubers (ICAR-CPRI seed plot technique).

healthy.name: Healthy
healthy.description: No disease or pest symptoms are visible on this potato leaf. Keep up balanced nutrition, regular irrigation and weekly scouting to keep the crop healthy.
symptoms: Uniform green colour
No spots, lesions, mottling, curling or webbing
